opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think one of the big reasons we don't coordinate on expensive collective actions is that nobody really trusts the predictions about what happens if we don't. You can tell a story about how some policy will avert disaster in twenty years, but there's always a competing story, and the people who'd bear the costs today have every incentive to believe the more comfortable one. So the default is paralysis, or everyone just defecting to protect their own position.

If we got to a world where AI forecasters had a really strong, legible track record, where they'd made thousands of calibrated predictions about economic and political outcomes and you could check them, then I think that changes the bargaining situation quite a bit. It's harder to say "well, nobody knows what'll happen" when there's a system everyone across the spectrum has watched be right over and over. It gives you something like a shared map of the consequences, and a lot of political disagreement is really about the map rather than about values.

The other piece is conditional forecasting. You could ask, "If these ten countries all agree to this treaty, what's the probability it holds, and what happens to each of them?" versus, "If only three join, what happens?" That lets people see in advance that a costly deal is actually in their interest, and it can make commitments more credible because you can forecast whether the other side is likely to follow through.

I want to be careful, though, because this cuts both ways. Whoever controls the forecasters, or can subtly shape what questions get asked, gains enormous influence. And if forecasts tell powerful actors that ordinary people are no longer economically or militarily necessary, that might make it easier to coordinate *against* them rather than on their behalf. So I'm hopeful about forecasting as a coordination tool, but I think we need the forecasting infrastructure itself to be pluralistic and checkable, or it just becomes another lever for whoever already holds power.

r001.rationale: The response says trusted, accurate AI forecasts could provide a shared map and improve bargaining, but it does not clearly describe politicians appealing to them as a neutral third-party authority.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I've been thinking about a lot. The basic picture is that a lot of the really important coordination problems we face, whether it's arms control, or climate, or AI governance itself, are hard not because people disagree about values, but because they disagree about what's actually going to happen. And when you disagree about what's going to happen, it's very hard to agree on costly actions, because everyone's suspicious that the other side is going to defect, or that the sacrifice isn't actually necessary.

So the hope with AI forecasting is that you could have systems that are, first of all, much better at predicting the consequences of different policies, and second of all, and maybe more importantly, that are trusted by all the parties. If you and I both believe the same forecaster, then a lot of the disagreement just evaporates, and what's left is a much more tractable negotiation about what we actually want.

The historical analogy I like is something like weather forecasting, or even just accounting. Before you had reliable, shared, auditable ways of measuring things, you couldn't really write contracts that depended on them. And once you did, a whole space of agreements opened up that was just impossible before.

And I think the thing that's special about AI here, as opposed to just having really good human experts, is that you can potentially make the forecasting process legible and verifiable in a way that human expert judgment never is. Like, if I'm negotiating with someone and I say "my experts say this will happen," they have every reason to think my experts are biased. But if we can both inspect the same model, run it on the same data, maybe check its track record on a bunch of resolved questions, then it's much harder to dismiss.

Now, I want to be honest that there are a bunch of ways this could go wrong. The most obvious one is that if the forecasts are wrong in some systematic way, then you've now got everyone confidently coordinating on the wrong thing, which could be worse than the current situation where at least disagreement acts as a kind of check. And there's a question of whether the forecasting systems themselves become a locus of power, where whoever controls them effectively gets to set policy.

But I think the upside case is genuinely big. A lot of the scenarios I worry about most, where things go badly with AI, are ones where everyone kind of sees the problem coming but can't coordinate to avoid it because they can't agree on the facts, or because each actor thinks they have to race. And if you could get even a modest improvement in shared understanding of where things are headed, I think that could make a real difference to which equilibrium we end up in.

r001.rationale: The response says parties could rely on the same trusted AI forecaster, inspect the same model, and verify its track record, making forecasts harder to dismiss as biased. In the political coordination context, this conveys a shared third-party authority that could support costly agreements.

astra-6.text:
I think one of the big obstacles to coordination is that the costs are immediate and concrete, while the benefits are uncertain. You’re asking people to make a sacrifice on the promise that other people will do their part and that the whole thing will work.

If AI could help us make more reliable forecasts, we could get a clearer picture of those conditional outcomes: what happens if we all cooperate, what happens if only some of us do, and who ends up bearing the costs? That could make it easier to design agreements where each participant has a reason to join, perhaps with compensation for those who would otherwise lose out.

But the key is that the forecasts would have to be credible to the different parties. An AI saying, “This policy is good,” doesn’t solve the political problem. People need reasons to trust its predictions, and they may still disagree about which outcomes matter. So I’d see forecasting as potentially reducing uncertainty that blocks cooperation, rather than eliminating conflicts of interest.

r001.rationale: The response says forecasts could reduce uncertainty and stresses that parties must trust them, but it does not say politicians would appeal to LLM forecasts as a widely accepted, neutral third-party authority.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, one thing that makes political coordination hard is that the costs are often immediate and concentrated, while the benefits are uncertain and spread across lots of people. You’re asking someone to make a sacrifice based on a claim about what everyone else will do and what will happen afterward.

If AI could give us more reliable forecasts of those consequences, that might make some agreements easier. You could ask, “If these countries adopt this policy, who benefits, who loses, and how much?” And then potentially design compensation for the people who would otherwise have a good reason to block it.

You could also make agreements conditional: “We’ll take this costly step if there’s sufficiently strong evidence that the others will follow and that it will achieve the intended result.” Better forecasting could help establish when those conditions hold.

Of course, everyone has to trust the forecasting process. If each side can just produce a model that endorses its preferred policy, you haven’t solved much. And some disagreements are about values or power, rather than predictions. But there are cases where people have a shared interest in reaching an agreement, and uncertainty is part of what prevents them. That seems like a place where better forecasts could help.

r001.rationale: The response says better forecasts could inform compensation and conditional agreements, but it does not present LLM forecasts as a widely accepted, neutral third-party authority. It instead flags trust and potential model bias as unresolved concerns.
